study_identification_part.si4_title: Judged by your neighbors: A novel framework for personalized assessment of brain structural aging effects in diverse populations

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To introduce Nearest Neighbor Normativity (N³), a novel framework designed to resolve the confound between natural diversity and subtle pathological patterns in brain structure, and to evaluate individual brain structures from multiple meaningful viewpoints while accommodating diverse normative prototypes and individually varying progression rates of brain structural decline.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Type III Sum of Squares ANOVA using ordinary least squares (OLS) model to assess discriminative and explanatory power, adjusted for age, age squared, sex, and scanner; partial eta squared (η²) for effect size quantification with 95% CI; post-hoc comparisons with permutation testing (1000 permutations) to test marker differences; Spearman's rank correlation for age bias assessment; machine learning classification with nested cross-validation (k=5 outer, k=10 inner folds) using SVM with Grid Search hyperparameter optimization; performance metrics include balanced accuracy, recall, precision, and F1-score; balanced sampling (random under-sampling) to address class imbalance.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: The N³ biomarker significantly outperformed conventional normative modeling approaches and brain age models in distinguishing neurodegenerative diseases from healthy controls, showing the largest effect sizes across MCI (η²=0.067), AD (η²=0.292), and FTD (η²=0.377), with superior balanced accuracy, F1-scores, and sensitivity in machine learning predictions.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: The N³ biomarker demonstrated superior discriminative ability across all neurodegenerative conditions tested. For Alzheimer's Disease, N³ showed the largest effect size (η²=0.29), explaining approximately 29% of variance between AD and controls, compared to η²=0.23 for NM-C, η²=0.21 for NM-S, and η²=0.08 for BAG. In Frontotemporal Dementia, N³ achieved an effect size of η²=0.38, substantially higher than all other markers. For Mild Cognitive Impairment, while all markers showed lower explanatory power, N³ demonstrated relative advantage with η²=0.07 versus η²=0.05 for BAG and η²=0.02 for normative modeling scores. In machine learning analyses, N³ achieved balanced accuracy improvements of 5.8% for AD and 7.5% for FTD compared to second-best markers. For MCI, N³ reached 1.1% improvement over BAG. N³ displayed superior sensitivity rates across all conditions (+1.6% for MCI, +11.0% for AD, +2.9% for FTD), with highest F1-scores demonstrating optimal balance of sensitivity and precision. The N³ marker showed no significant correlation with age (ρ not significant) in healthy controls, indicating consistency across age groups, while BAG exhibited moderate age bias (ρ=0.21, p<0.001) even after bias correction. Stability analysis using downsampled NAKO subsets showed that N³ achieved high stability (ICC ≥0.75) with samples of 200+ individuals and excellent stability (ICC ≥0.90) with 300+ participants, validated on external MACS (n=835) and ADNI (n=1073) datasets.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The authors emphasize that the N³ framework is designed for precision medicine applications and can be adapted to various medical domains beyond brain structure by customizing the density estimation algorithm, distance metrics, or dimensionality reduction techniques. They note potential clinical applications include: (1) attachment to routine MRI scans for early detection of neurodegenerative diseases before clinical symptoms appear, (2) comprehensive assessment of neurostructural alterations associated with specific symptoms to understand disease etiology, (3) measuring impact of environmental factors, treatment options, and neuroinflammatory processes for optimized disease management, and (4) biomarker validation in neuropsychiatric research. The authors plan to extend the approach to process different MRI tissue contrasts and evaluate deep-learning based embeddings to optimize information gain, and to investigate relationships with genetic risk factors. Code for the N³ framework will be made available as open-source on GitHub.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: The N³ framework requires larger sample sizes compared to traditional approaches, with stability analysis showing that at least 200-300 individuals are needed for reliable estimates, which may not be feasible in smaller clinical studies; the effectiveness relies on the choice of density estimation algorithm and the k parameter (set to 10% of control group size, capped at 15 in this study); the current application used only five global brain volume measures (GM, WM, WMH, CSF, TIV), which are broad aggregates and may not capture fine-grained regional or network-level variations; training was performed on a single cohort (NAKO) which may limit generalizability despite validation on multiple external datasets; no explicit quality control procedures were described for the imaging data; site effects were addressed only minimally by including scanner as a covariate in statistical analyses rather than using dedicated harmonization methods.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is a preprint (medRxiv) posted June 18, 2025, not yet peer-reviewed. The study represents a novel methodological contribution introducing the Nearest Neighbor Normativity (N³) framework, which differs fundamentally from traditional normative modeling approaches. Key innovations include: (1) demographic contextualization through stratified control groups, (2) accommodation of multiple normative prototypes via local density estimation rather than single population averages, (3) normativity profiles providing multi-perspective assessments across the aging continuum, and (4) meta-normativity synthesis into a single actionable biomarker. The framework was developed with data from 36,896 individuals total (29,883 for training, 7,013 for testing across multiple neurodegenerative conditions). The study involved multiple large consortia: NAKO, ADNI, AIBL, NIFD, OASIS3, and MACS. Training data came exclusively from NAKO (German National Cohort), a population-based longitudinal study. The approach uses exponentiated Weibull distribution to model the distribution of local density estimates, which provides flexibility for various distributional shapes. The k parameter (number of neighbors for density estimation) was set to 10% of control group size with an upper bound of 15 to prevent overly broad comparisons while maintaining robustness. The framework creates 100 control groups stratified by sex and age (ages 22-72 years, same-aged males or females). For underrepresented age groups, neighboring age groups were combined to approximate median sample size per sex. The comparison normative modeling approaches used PCNtoolkit with Bayesian Linear Regression, and Brain Age models used Support Vector Machines implemented in photonai with nested cross-validation and age bias correction following Peng et al. All statistical analyses were implemented in Python using scipy, statsmodels, and pingouin libraries. The correlation between N³ and BAG was moderate-to-strong (ρ=0.65), while correlations with normative modeling markers were weaker (0.19 < |ρ| < 0.25), suggesting N³ captures different aspects of brain structural normativity.
